title: Sourcing and using compost in a rooftop garden
subtitle: Managing weight limits and compost quality when you are growing above ground level
excerpt: A rooftop garden grows in containers or raised beds with no connection to ground soil. The growing medium degrades faster than in-ground beds and must be replenished from an external source. Weight, drainage, and the absence of earthworms shape every decision about what compost to use.
sourceNotes: British Standard BS 8616 on growing media; RHS guidance on container growing; GRO Green Roof Code on growing media specification for extensive and intensive green roofs.

glossaryTerms.definition: A growing medium or compost that contains no peat, using alternatives such as coir, bark, green compost, or wood fibre to provide structure and moisture retention.
The solid excretions of compost worms, a finished, fine-textured compost with a higher available nutrient content than standard compost.

content.text: Rooftop containers and raised beds compact and lose fertility faster than in-ground beds. There are no earthworms to cycle material. There is no subsoil to buffer drying. Regular irrigation flushes nutrients out quickly. The two maintenance tasks are annual top-dressing and periodic medium replacement.

A structural rooftop typically carries 150 to 250 kg/m² of imposed load. A standard peat-free growing medium weighs approximately 350 to 500 kg/m³ when saturated. A 200 mm deep raised bed of standard compost weighs 70 to 100 kg/m² when wet. For many rooftops, that is close to the structural limit. Never add compost to a rooftop growing system without confirming the roof's imposed-load rating with a structural engineer.
Green roof extensive medium: crushed brick and perlite with 15 to 20% organic material. Weighs 90 to 130 kg/m³ dry.
and drains freely. Only suitable for drought-tolerant plants.
Perlite and coir mix: 1 part perlite to 2 parts coir by volume. Approximately 200 to 280 kg/m³ saturated. Needs regular liquid feeding as it holds few nutrients on its own.
Commercial lightweight growing media (e.g. Seramis, expanded clay aggregate mixes): specifically designed for container growing with reduced wet weight.
In spring, apply a 20 to 30 mm layer of mature
or green compost to the top of each container. Do not dig it in, surface application allows it to mix in gradually without disturbing roots.
Every 3 to 4 years, replace 30 to 50% of the growing medium in permanent containers. Remove old compacted medium and replace with fresh lightweight mix.
Sourcing compost without a ground garden
Council green-waste compost: most UK councils sell PAS 100-certified green compost by the bag or bulk bag. Call the local depot, bulk bags are usually cheaper per litre than garden-centre bags.

Wormery on the roof or balcony: a stacking wormery processes kitchen waste into castings in the same space where the growing happens. Even a single small wormery produces enough castings to top-dress 2 to 4 m² of growing area per year.

rows.symptom: Growing medium sags and compacts within one season
rows.cause: High proportion of fine compost particles settling under repeated irrigation; no structural amendment
rows.fix: Mix in 20 to 30% perlite or fine grit by volume when replacing the medium. This keeps drainage channels open as organic matter breaks down.
